Oncofertility

By: Laura Byrne | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Cancer is an ordeal that leaves little time to consider long-distant futures like having children - but fertility experts are working to preserve fertility for young people undergoing chemotherapy.

Unique Selling Point:
Oncofertility is a new and rapidly developing field. The term was coined in 2006 by Dr Teresa Woodruff, who realised the need for a coordinated effort to preserve the fertility of young people who undergo chemotherapy before they've had a chance to conceive a child - or even consider whether they want to be parents. In two short decades, the field has seen ground-breaking innovations: live births from preserved ovarian tissue; preserving testicular and ovarian tissue from prepubertal girls and boys; and (in the pipeline) development of bio-prosthetic ovaries.

Summary:
Fertility preservation has always been easy for men, who can simply freeze sperm - a process which is quick and easy, and no different from an ordinary IVF procedure. However in the early 2000s, US researcher Dr Teresa Woodruff found women were rarely offered options as they were so limited. In some circumstances, women can harvest oocytes in the same way as they would to undergo IVF. However, if they are pre-puberty or the cancer is advanced and treatment is urgent so they can't wait for the required hormonal process, this is not an option. Instead, women can now cryopreserve ovarian tissue, which can later be implanted (even without ovaries), allowing oocytes to be harvested later and fertilised. Amazingly, in many cases, women actually have a spontaneous pregnancy once the tissue is implanted. So far, there have been over 200 live births from this procedure: a massive acceleration since the first birth in 2004. In fact, the procedure has recently had its "experimental" designation removed.

The huge added benefit is that the ovarian tissue also helps with hormone regulation: our ovaries produce the oestrogen and progesterone that women need for normal hormone function. Chemotherapy can destroy the oocytes and bring on premature menopause, which means younger women often have to spend the rest of their lives on hormone replacement therapy. Ovarian tissue transplant can restore normal function and prevent this. (This is not the case with men: destruction of the sperm cells does not stop testosterone production so there is no need for HRT).

Our story will look at the origins and successes of the field of oncofertility, interviewing international and local experts, as well as case studies - with a particular focus on the emergence of fertility preservation options for paediatric patients.

Further information:
CASE STUDIES
1. In South Africa, Lee Anne Williams was the first woman - and so far, still the only one - to give birth following an ovarian tissue transplant. She was diagnosed with Hodgkins lymphoma in 2008 - an aggressive form of cancer that required immediate treatment. She had no time for oocyte harvest and instead had one ovary removed, preserved, and a tiny piece of tissue later re-implanted onto her remaining ovary. She fell pregnant spontaneously and quickly, and in 2013 she gave birth to her son, Zachariah. Carte Blanche covered the story in 2014. Today Zachariah the "miracle child" is thriving. Lee Anne experienced symptoms of menopause which disappeared with the transplant, but have recently returned. She is considering a second transplant to restore her hormonal function.

2. Little Mackenzie Harrington Johnson turned one on 5 January 2022. Her short life has not been easy. At just four months, she was diagnosed with cancer. At eight months, she underwent surgery to have an ovary removed and preserved before undergoing stem cell transplant, for which she is currently in hospital. At less than a year old, it's almost impossible to consider whether Mackenzie will want children, but the stem cell transplant will 'kill' her ovaries, which are each just a centimetre or two long. Of course, Mackenzie has years before she will hit puberty, so her ovarian tissue is immature, which means that oocyte removal would never have been possible. Amazingly, it will be entirely possible to preserve the tissue from her ovary for the decades ahead in which she will grow up and make the decision for herself; in addition, should the cancer treatment damage her ovaries irreversibly, she might experience developmental difficulties when she reaches the age of puberty: the transplanted tissue will restore her hormone function and may allow her to avoid taking hormone replacement therapy for the rest of her life.

Oncofertility is becoming more and more important as cancer diagnoses are increasing - but so are survival rates. Children especially are resilient and have a more than 80% survival rate. But if a 10 year-old undergoes chemotherapy and survives, his or her choice to become a parent in 20 years time is often simultaneously taken away. So paediatric fertility preservation is a central focus of oncofertility. Mackenzie is an example of fertility preservation for a (very) prepubertal girl. This procedure has only led to about two live births worldwide, partly because the patients are young and the science is new, so very few have yet reached childbearing age.

In prepubertal boys, research is ongoing to pioneer the preservation and reimplantation of testicular tissue. So far, scientists have achieved a live birth in a non-human primate but there has been no human live birth as yet and the procedure remains extremely experimental.

There is a risk in some types of cancer that reimplanting ovarian tissue may "reinfect" the patient with cancer. There is research ongoing to mature tissue and oocytes in vitro to prevent this, but follicles are extremely delicate and collapse in petri dish conditions. Woodruff and her team are currently researching 3D printed bio-prosthetic ovaries that will mimic the 3D structure of the original ovary and allow for maturation of tissue and eggs.

The applications of oncofertility are also expanding. For example, people undergoing gender-confirmation surgery may wish to preserve their gonadal tissue to keep the option of having biological children in the future.

Dr Woodruff not only established the term and field of oncofertility, but founded an international Oncofertility Consortium, which brings together oncologists and fertility specialists around the world, and aims to make fertility preservation more widely available and more affordable. Members see these procedures as philanthropic exercises, and so treatment (while still expensive) is often provided at cost. Dr Chris Venter got in touch with Dr Woodruff in 2017 and entered South Africa into the Oncofertility Consortium.

Press Release:


A story of ground-breaking innovation in medicine that’s meeting a deep human desire: to have children. And doing it for young people diagnosed with life-threatening cancers. Around the world, a collective of scientists is helping families preserve the future fertility of their children from the ravages of chemotherapy. Carte Blanche meets one-year-old Mackenzie “Mighty Mack” Friedman, diagnosed with aggressive leukaemia at just four months old. She recently underwent surgery to remove and preserve one of her tiny ovaries before undergoing a bone marrow transplant. The growing field of oncofertility is addressing two of the most time-sensitive aspects of this little girl’s life – getting urgent cancer treatment and preserving her chance to have a baby of her own one day.

Script:


UPSOUND: LEE-ANNE SCULLARD: Say Carte Blanche is here to do a follow-up interview from the last one in 2014. And smile! Don’t forget to smile.

VO: Zachary Williams is eight years old. He loves to dance and his favourite superhero is Spiderman.

UPSOUND: LEE-ANNE SCULLARD: Zachary's vibrant, hyperactive. He's a very caring child, very sensitive child. He’s very bright at school.

VO: When Carte Blanche last met Zachary and his mom, Lee Anne Scullard, he was just a baby…

UPSOUND LEE-ANNE SCULLARD-WILLIAMS [CARTE BLANCHE 2014]: And when I saw him I just cried and I thought thank the lord for this miracle baby. He is so beautiful.

VO: And there is something that sets Zachary apart.

UPSOUND: ZACHARY WILLIAMS: My mommy preserved…ovarian…tissue.

VO: Chemotherapy to treat her aggressive cancer left Lee Anne infertile. But preserving her ovarian tissue allowed her to fall pregnant with Zachary. The first such birth in South Africa, it was a landmark event in an emerging field called oncofertility.

UPSOUND: DR TERESA WOODRUFF: It really was one of those great things in science and medicine, which is an aha moment, that led me to imagine that we should really blend these two major fields of oncology and fertility.

VO: The word was coined in 2006 by celebrated reproductive scientist, Dr Teresa Woodruff, then at Northwestern University, Illinois.

UPSOUND: DR TERESA WOODRUFF: Someone indicated to me that a 14 year old boy had just been brought down from our children's hospital to attempt to bank sperm because they thought he would lose fertility.
And I said, Well, that's just fantastic. What do we do for the young women? And that physician said, Oh, well, they really shouldn't worry about that. They need to really focus on their cancer. And I thought, Well, that doesn't quite make sense.

VO: Seeing a gap, Woodruff founded an international network of specialists called the Oncofertility Consortium.

UPSOUND: DR TERESA WOODRUFF: At the outset, it was clear that if all we did was to create scientific breakthroughs, and we wrote a paper for the New England Journal of Medicine, got a grant and started all over again, that would be great, maybe for one or two individuals. But the question was how could this really become a broader impact to people living literally around the globe?

UPSOUND: PROF GEORGIA DEMETRIOU: It's a conversation I have with all my patients who still are young and want fertility and are potentially curative.

VO: Professor Georgia Demetriou is the academic head of oncology at Wits University.

UPSOUND: PROF GEORGIA DEMETRIOU: For example, the highest incidence of Hodgkin's is round about age 12 to 25. You know, those people are just starting their lives. You can often cure the cancer, but you don't want them then, in their late 20s, 30s, when they may be ready to have a family, to suddenly realise, But we didn't discuss fertility. And you never really get a second chance at that apple.

VO: Oncofertility calls on some familiar techniques: sperm banking for male patients; egg harvesting for females; and embryo preservation for couples.
But as childhood cancer survival rates skyrocket, the focus has shifted to much younger patients.
This deceptively normal family scene depends on some very futuristic medical science. Megan Harrington Johnson and Bronson Friedman are adjusting to life outside the Intensive Care Unit with their daughter, Mackenzie.

UPSOUND: MEGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: She was perfectly healthy when she was born. She was on weight, on track. For the first four months of her life, she was doing all the things that she was supposed to do…
MASA KEKANA: When do you realise something is wrong?
BRONSON FRIEDMAN: I was playing golf on a Saturday. Megs phoned me, she said that Mackenzie is battling a fever. I said cool, maybe take her to the GP…

VO: The next day, blood tests revealed that what looked like an ordinary infection was something much more frightening…and ushered Mackenzie into the care of paediatric oncologist Dr Nadia Beringer.

UPSOUND: DR NADIA BERINGER: Mack was a seemingly healthy, beautiful four month old girl who had been admitted with a fever of unknown origin. I performed a bone marrow biopsy, which confirmed the diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia.

UPSOUND: BRONSON FRIEDMAN: I suppose you’re just shocked. Can't be us. What are we going to do?
MEGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: And you also hear that word cancer and you immediately think it's a death sentence.

VO: What followed was a desperate battle for Mackenzie’s life. Her aggressive leukaemia could only be treated with a bone marrow transplant: a lifesaving procedure with long-term consequences.

#MIGHTYMACK VIDEO: EGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: Guess what? I’m in remission!

UPSOUND: DR NADIA BERINGER: The chemo that children get when they are undergoing a bone marrow transplant is myeloablative. So that means it actually obliterates your own bone marrow before accepting a donor bone marrow. And so that extremely strong chemotherapy will most likely render the child infertile.

LINK: MASA KEKANA: When your baby girl is not even a year old yet, probably the furthest thing from your mind is the children that she will have one day. But in the case of little Mackenzie Friedman, that was a conversation thrust upon her parents very early in her short life.

UPSOUND: MASA KEKANA: So when did the conversation then move to preserving Mackenzie's facility?
MEGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: Quite late in the process. It was very much back of mind. We really actually just wanted her to survive.
BRONSON FRIEDMAN: In saying that, I've seen Megs and a few other friends battle with fertility problems. And if there was even a slight possibility that we could give her the opportunity at a later stage to not have to go through these problems, that would be first prize.
MEGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: Once you have kids of your own, you realise how life-changing it is to have your own child. And we wanted to be able to give her that opportunity.

UPSOUND: DR CHRIS VENTER: Where someone has been sort of in despair, just to say, well, currently you're in a bad space, but let's just for a moment think about the future. So we're offering them that hope for the future.

VO: Mackenzie is the youngest patient referred to fertility specialist Dr Chris Venter, who brought South Africa into the Oncofertility Consortium in 2018.

UPSOUND: DR CHRIS VENTER: Here we have something like oncology that is associated with despair and something like fertility that represents new life.

VO: Protecting Mackenzie’s fertility meant a procedure that has until recently been considered experimental even in adult women: ovarian tissue cryopreservation.
Maturing and harvesting eggs takes about 12 days: time some women can’t afford to wait before they start chemotherapy. Ovarian tissue cryopreservation can be done in just a day or two.
Mackenzie is years away from puberty, which means egg harvesting is impossible. So last November, one of her pea-sized ovaries was removed and preserved.

UPSOUND: EMBRYOLOGIST: This is a full ovary. You can even see the follicles on the outer layer.
MASA KEKANA: If it were a human ovary, would the size be relatively the same?
EMBRYOLOGIST: It would be smaller.

LINK: MASA KEKANA: This is bovine tissue – a cow ovary. Our fertility specialists have kindly allowed us to film the process of preserving ovarian tissue – but of course we can’t have our cameras getting in the way of a real medical procedure. So this bovine ovary will be our stand-in.

UPSOUND: MASA KEKANA: You need extreme concentration.
EMBRYOLOGIST: And at the back of your mind you’re also aware that this is a child’s hope.

VO: The follicles, containing immature egg cells, are in the ovary’s outer layer, so this part must be preserved.

UPSOUND: DR CHRIS VENTER: When will we find out if it’s going to be effective? And we will only find out in, let’s say Mackenzie’s case, in 20 years from now.
MASA KEKANA: Sjoe. It’s a long wait and see game.
EMBRYOLOGIST: Now we’re going to start cutting it into strips…

VO: Any remaining tissue is examined to assess the number of follicles present - and whether it contains cancer cells that could be reimplanted later.
The strips are placed in a protective solution, then slowly frozen.

UPSOUND: MASA KEKANA: And this is where it will spend the rest of its life until that patient decides they want to start a family.
EMBRYOLOGIST: Yes, exactly correct.

VO: In theory, there’s no limit on how long Mackenzie’s tissue will remain viable.

UPSOUND: DR CHRIS VENTER: Once she wants to start her family, we will just go and implant some of these grafts within the site where we removed the previous ovary.
Within a three to five month period, this ovarian tissue will then start functioning and will then start producing eggs.

VO: The reimplanted tissue will also produce hormones, allowing Mackenzie to have a normal menstrual cycle.
Oncofertility research is constantly developing new insurance plans for the survivors of the future.

UPSOUND: DR NADIA BERINGER: I've recently referred my youngest patient who was eight weeks old. Because of his age, he will require a testicular biopsy. And this is even more experimental. To date there has been no live births from preserved testicular tissue in prepubertal children.

VO: Ovarian tissue cryopreservation has yielded over 200 births worldwide to date, but Zachary remains the only one in South Africa.

UPSOUND: ZACHARY WILLIAMS: I'm very happy that I'm born and my mommy went through a lot. If she didn't, I wouldn't be here right now.

UPSOUND: LEE-ANNE SCULLARD: It gives me peace of mind knowing that I can go back any time and have the same procedure done.

VO: It’s hard to imagine what will be possible when Mackenzie might return for her tissue…

UPSOUND: MEGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: The fact that we were able to protect her future children and our future grandchildren one day is really incredible.

PROMO 1 (21 SECONDS)

VO: What do you do when doctors tell you that your 8 month-old baby girl might never be able to have children?

UPSOUND: BRONSON FRIEDMAN: I've seen Megs battle with fertility problems. And if there was even a slight possibility that we could give her the opportunity to not have to go through these problems, that would be first prize.

VO: Thanks to a cutting-edge medical procedure, baby Mackenzie may still have that choice.

PROMO 2 (21 SECONDS)

UPSOUND: MASA KEKANA: I feel like I’m holding something so sensitive and sacred.
EMBRYOLOGIST: That’s where life begins.

VO: Oncology and fertility seem worlds apart: one associated with death and the other with new life. But that’s changing.

PROMO 3 (11 SECONDS)

VO: At less than a year old, baby Mackenzie almost lost the chance to one day have her own children. But a remarkable medical intervention has literally preserved her choice.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 31 March 2022 Press Release: A story of ground-breaking innovation in medicine that’s meeting a deep human desire: to have children. And doing it for young people diagnosed with life-threatening cancers. Around the world, a collective of scientists is helping families preserve the future fertility of their children from the ravages of chemotherapy. Carte Blanche meets one-year-old Mackenzie “Mighty Mack” Friedman, diagnosed with aggressive leukaemia at just four months old. She recently underwent surgery to remove and preserve one of her tiny ovaries before undergoing a bone marrow transplant. The growing field of oncofertility is addressing two of the most time-sensitive aspects of this little girl’s life – getting urgent cancer treatment and preserving her chance to have a baby of her own one day. Script: UPSOUND: LEE-ANNE SCULLARD: Say Carte Blanche is here to do a follow-up interview from the last one in 2014. And smile! Don’t forget to smile. VO: Zachary Williams is eight years old. He loves to dance and his favourite superhero is Spiderman. UPSOUND: LEE-ANNE SCULLARD: Zachary's vibrant, hyperactive. He's a very caring child, very sensitive child. He’s very bright at school. VO: When Carte Blanche last met Zachary and his mom, Lee Anne Scullard, he was just a baby… UPSOUND LEE-ANNE SCULLARD-WILLIAMS [CARTE BLANCHE 2014]: And when I saw him I just cried and I thought thank the lord for this miracle baby. He is so beautiful. VO: And there is something that sets Zachary apart. UPSOUND: ZACHARY WILLIAMS: My mommy preserved…ovarian…tissue. VO: Chemotherapy to treat her aggressive cancer left Lee Anne infertile. But preserving her ovarian tissue allowed her to fall pregnant with Zachary. The first such birth in South Africa, it was a landmark event in an emerging field called oncofertility. UPSOUND: DR TERESA WOODRUFF: It really was one of those great things in science and medicine, which is an aha moment, that led me to imagine that we should really blend these two major fields of oncology and fertility. VO: The word was coined in 2006 by celebrated reproductive scientist, Dr Teresa Woodruff, then at Northwestern University, Illinois. UPSOUND: DR TERESA WOODRUFF: Someone indicated to me that a 14 year old boy had just been brought down from our children's hospital to attempt to bank sperm because they thought he would lose fertility. And I said, Well, that's just fantastic. What do we do for the young women? And that physician said, Oh, well, they really shouldn't worry about that. They need to really focus on their cancer. And I thought, Well, that doesn't quite make sense. VO: Seeing a gap, Woodruff founded an international network of specialists called the Oncofertility Consortium. UPSOUND: DR TERESA WOODRUFF: At the outset, it was clear that if all we did was to create scientific breakthroughs, and we wrote a paper for the New England Journal of Medicine, got a grant and started all over again, that would be great, maybe for one or two individuals. But the question was how could this really become a broader impact to people living literally around the globe? UPSOUND: PROF GEORGIA DEMETRIOU: It's a conversation I have with all my patients who still are young and want fertility and are potentially curative. VO: Professor Georgia Demetriou is the academic head of oncology at Wits University. UPSOUND: PROF GEORGIA DEMETRIOU: For example, the highest incidence of Hodgkin's is round about age 12 to 25. You know, those people are just starting their lives. You can often cure the cancer, but you don't want them then, in their late 20s, 30s, when they may be ready to have a family, to suddenly realise, But we didn't discuss fertility. And you never really get a second chance at that apple. VO: Oncofertility calls on some familiar techniques: sperm banking for male patients; egg harvesting for females; and embryo preservation for couples. But as childhood cancer survival rates skyrocket, the focus has shifted to much younger patients. This deceptively normal family scene depends on some very futuristic medical science. Megan Harrington Johnson and Bronson Friedman are adjusting to life outside the Intensive Care Unit with their daughter, Mackenzie. UPSOUND: MEGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: She was perfectly healthy when she was born. She was on weight, on track. For the first four months of her life, she was doing all the things that she was supposed to do… MASA KEKANA: When do you realise something is wrong? BRONSON FRIEDMAN: I was playing golf on a Saturday. Megs phoned me, she said that Mackenzie is battling a fever. I said cool, maybe take her to the GP… VO: The next day, blood tests revealed that what looked like an ordinary infection was something much more frightening…and ushered Mackenzie into the care of paediatric oncologist Dr Nadia Beringer. UPSOUND: DR NADIA BERINGER: Mack was a seemingly healthy, beautiful four month old girl who had been admitted with a fever of unknown origin. I performed a bone marrow biopsy, which confirmed the diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia. UPSOUND: BRONSON FRIEDMAN: I suppose you’re just shocked. Can't be us. What are we going to do? MEGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: And you also hear that word cancer and you immediately think it's a death sentence. VO: What followed was a desperate battle for Mackenzie’s life. Her aggressive leukaemia could only be treated with a bone marrow transplant: a lifesaving procedure with long-term consequences. #MIGHTYMACK VIDEO: EGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: Guess what? I’m in remission! UPSOUND: DR NADIA BERINGER: The chemo that children get when they are undergoing a bone marrow transplant is myeloablative. So that means it actually obliterates your own bone marrow before accepting a donor bone marrow. And so that extremely strong chemotherapy will most likely render the child infertile. LINK: MASA KEKANA: When your baby girl is not even a year old yet, probably the furthest thing from your mind is the children that she will have one day. But in the case of little Mackenzie Friedman, that was a conversation thrust upon her parents very early in her short life. UPSOUND: MASA KEKANA: So when did the conversation then move to preserving Mackenzie's facility? MEGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: Quite late in the process. It was very much back of mind. We really actually just wanted her to survive. BRONSON FRIEDMAN: In saying that, I've seen Megs and a few other friends battle with fertility problems. And if there was even a slight possibility that we could give her the opportunity at a later stage to not have to go through these problems, that would be first prize. MEGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: Once you have kids of your own, you realise how life-changing it is to have your own child. And we wanted to be able to give her that opportunity. UPSOUND: DR CHRIS VENTER: Where someone has been sort of in despair, just to say, well, currently you're in a bad space, but let's just for a moment think about the future. So we're offering them that hope for the future. VO: Mackenzie is the youngest patient referred to fertility specialist Dr Chris Venter, who brought South Africa into the Oncofertility Consortium in 2018. UPSOUND: DR CHRIS VENTER: Here we have something like oncology that is associated with despair and something like fertility that represents new life. VO: Protecting Mackenzie’s fertility meant a procedure that has until recently been considered experimental even in adult women: ovarian tissue cryopreservation. Maturing and harvesting eggs takes about 12 days: time some women can’t afford to wait before they start chemotherapy. Ovarian tissue cryopreservation can be done in just a day or two. Mackenzie is years away from puberty, which means egg harvesting is impossible. So last November, one of her pea-sized ovaries was removed and preserved. UPSOUND: EMBRYOLOGIST: This is a full ovary. You can even see the follicles on the outer layer. MASA KEKANA: If it were a human ovary, would the size be relatively the same? EMBRYOLOGIST: It would be smaller. LINK: MASA KEKANA: This is bovine tissue – a cow ovary. Our fertility specialists have kindly allowed us to film the process of preserving ovarian tissue – but of course we can’t have our cameras getting in the way of a real medical procedure. So this bovine ovary will be our stand-in. UPSOUND: MASA KEKANA: You need extreme concentration. EMBRYOLOGIST: And at the back of your mind you’re also aware that this is a child’s hope. VO: The follicles, containing immature egg cells, are in the ovary’s outer layer, so this part must be preserved. UPSOUND: DR CHRIS VENTER: When will we find out if it’s going to be effective? And we will only find out in, let’s say Mackenzie’s case, in 20 years from now. MASA KEKANA: Sjoe. It’s a long wait and see game. EMBRYOLOGIST: Now we’re going to start cutting it into strips… VO: Any remaining tissue is examined to assess the number of follicles present - and whether it contains cancer cells that could be reimplanted later. The strips are placed in a protective solution, then slowly frozen. UPSOUND: MASA KEKANA: And this is where it will spend the rest of its life until that patient decides they want to start a family. EMBRYOLOGIST: Yes, exactly correct. VO: In theory, there’s no limit on how long Mackenzie’s tissue will remain viable. UPSOUND: DR CHRIS VENTER: Once she wants to start her family, we will just go and implant some of these grafts within the site where we removed the previous ovary. Within a three to five month period, this ovarian tissue will then start functioning and will then start producing eggs. VO: The reimplanted tissue will also produce hormones, allowing Mackenzie to have a normal menstrual cycle. Oncofertility research is constantly developing new insurance plans for the survivors of the future. UPSOUND: DR NADIA BERINGER: I've recently referred my youngest patient who was eight weeks old. Because of his age, he will require a testicular biopsy. And this is even more experimental. To date there has been no live births from preserved testicular tissue in prepubertal children. VO: Ovarian tissue cryopreservation has yielded over 200 births worldwide to date, but Zachary remains the only one in South Africa. UPSOUND: ZACHARY WILLIAMS: I'm very happy that I'm born and my mommy went through a lot. If she didn't, I wouldn't be here right now. UPSOUND: LEE-ANNE SCULLARD: It gives me peace of mind knowing that I can go back any time and have the same procedure done. VO: It’s hard to imagine what will be possible when Mackenzie might return for her tissue… UPSOUND: MEGAN HARRINGTON-JOHNSON: The fact that we were able to protect her future children and our future grandchildren one day is really incredible. PROMO 1 (21 SECONDS) VO: What do you do when doctors tell you that your 8 month-old baby girl might never be able to have children? UPSOUND: BRONSON FRIEDMAN: I've seen Megs battle with fertility problems. And if there was even a slight possibility that we could give her the opportunity to not have to go through these problems, that would be first prize. VO: Thanks to a cutting-edge medical procedure, baby Mackenzie may still have that choice. PROMO 2 (21 SECONDS) UPSOUND: MASA KEKANA: I feel like I’m holding something so sensitive and sacred. EMBRYOLOGIST: That’s where life begins. VO: Oncology and fertility seem worlds apart: one associated with death and the other with new life. But that’s changing. PROMO 3 (11 SECONDS) VO: At less than a year old, baby Mackenzie almost lost the chance to one day have her own children. But a remarkable medical intervention has literally preserved her choice.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Cancer is an ordeal that leaves little time to consider long-distant futures like having children - but fertility experts are working to preserve fertility for young people undergoing chemotherapy.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Oncofertility is a new and rapidly developing field. The term was coined in 2006 by Dr Teresa Woodruff, who realised the need for a coordinated effort to preserve the fertility of young people who undergo chemotherapy before they've had a chance to conceive a child - or even consider whether they want to be parents. In two short decades, the field has seen ground-breaking innovations: live births from preserved ovarian tissue; preserving testicular and ovarian tissue from prepubertal girls and boys; and (in the pipeline) development of bio-prosthetic ovaries.
metadata.Summary: Fertility preservation has always been easy for men, who can simply freeze sperm - a process which is quick and easy, and no different from an ordinary IVF procedure. However in the early 2000s, US researcher Dr Teresa Woodruff found women were rarely offered options as they were so limited. In some circumstances, women can harvest oocytes in the same way as they would to undergo IVF. However, if they are pre-puberty or the cancer is advanced and treatment is urgent so they can't wait for the required hormonal process, this is not an option. Instead, women can now cryopreserve ovarian tissue, which can later be implanted (even without ovaries), allowing oocytes to be harvested later and fertilised. Amazingly, in many cases, women actually have a spontaneous pregnancy once the tissue is implanted. So far, there have been over 200 live births from this procedure: a massive acceleration since the first birth in 2004. In fact, the procedure has recently had its "experimental" designation removed. The huge added benefit is that the ovarian tissue also helps with hormone regulation: our ovaries produce the oestrogen and progesterone that women need for normal hormone function. Chemotherapy can destroy the oocytes and bring on premature menopause, which means younger women often have to spend the rest of their lives on hormone replacement therapy. Ovarian tissue transplant can restore normal function and prevent this. (This is not the case with men: destruction of the sperm cells does not stop testosterone production so there is no need for HRT). Our story will look at the origins and successes of the field of oncofertility, interviewing international and local experts, as well as case studies - with a particular focus on the emergence of fertility preservation options for paediatric patients.
metadata.Further information: CASE STUDIES 1. In South Africa, Lee Anne Williams was the first woman - and so far, still the only one - to give birth following an ovarian tissue transplant. She was diagnosed with Hodgkins lymphoma in 2008 - an aggressive form of cancer that required immediate treatment. She had no time for oocyte harvest and instead had one ovary removed, preserved, and a tiny piece of tissue later re-implanted onto her remaining ovary. She fell pregnant spontaneously and quickly, and in 2013 she gave birth to her son, Zachariah. Carte Blanche covered the story in 2014. Today Zachariah the "miracle child" is thriving. Lee Anne experienced symptoms of menopause which disappeared with the transplant, but have recently returned. She is considering a second transplant to restore her hormonal function. 2. Little Mackenzie Harrington Johnson turned one on 5 January 2022. Her short life has not been easy. At just four months, she was diagnosed with cancer. At eight months, she underwent surgery to have an ovary removed and preserved before undergoing stem cell transplant, for which she is currently in hospital. At less than a year old, it's almost impossible to consider whether Mackenzie will want children, but the stem cell transplant will 'kill' her ovaries, which are each just a centimetre or two long. Of course, Mackenzie has years before she will hit puberty, so her ovarian tissue is immature, which means that oocyte removal would never have been possible. Amazingly, it will be entirely possible to preserve the tissue from her ovary for the decades ahead in which she will grow up and make the decision for herself; in addition, should the cancer treatment damage her ovaries irreversibly, she might experience developmental difficulties when she reaches the age of puberty: the transplanted tissue will restore her hormone function and may allow her to avoid taking hormone replacement therapy for the rest of her life. Oncofertility is becoming more and more important as cancer diagnoses are increasing - but so are survival rates. Children especially are resilient and have a more than 80% survival rate. But if a 10 year-old undergoes chemotherapy and survives, his or her choice to become a parent in 20 years time is often simultaneously taken away. So paediatric fertility preservation is a central focus of oncofertility. Mackenzie is an example of fertility preservation for a (very) prepubertal girl. This procedure has only led to about two live births worldwide, partly because the patients are young and the science is new, so very few have yet reached childbearing age. In prepubertal boys, research is ongoing to pioneer the preservation and reimplantation of testicular tissue. So far, scientists have achieved a live birth in a non-human primate but there has been no human live birth as yet and the procedure remains extremely experimental. There is a risk in some types of cancer that reimplanting ovarian tissue may "reinfect" the patient with cancer. There is research ongoing to mature tissue and oocytes in vitro to prevent this, but follicles are extremely delicate and collapse in petri dish conditions. Woodruff and her team are currently researching 3D printed bio-prosthetic ovaries that will mimic the 3D structure of the original ovary and allow for maturation of tissue and eggs. The applications of oncofertility are also expanding. For example, people undergoing gender-confirmation surgery may wish to preserve their gonadal tissue to keep the option of having biological children in the future. Dr Woodruff not only established the term and field of oncofertility, but founded an international Oncofertility Consortium, which brings together oncologists and fertility specialists around the world, and aims to make fertility preservation more widely available and more affordable. Members see these procedures as philanthropic exercises, and so treatment (while still expensive) is often provided at cost. Dr Chris Venter got in touch with Dr Woodruff in 2017 and entered South Africa into the Oncofertility Consortium.
